method: remote camera traps (Reconyx Hyperfire H500, P800 and P900 on trees at 1 m, facing game trails or open areas); daily activity patterns per season from detections; overlap with bison estimated as coefficient D4
conditions: Free-ranging elk inside fenced Elk Island National Park, Alberta, Canada (2.2 m perimeter fence restricting movement of large mammals in and out; elk density 3-4 per km2 from aerial surveys; translocations no longer allowed and no elk removed during the study). Camera trapping December 2016 to October 2020 at 43 sites (31 in EINP-N, 12 in EINP-S, systematic 2 x 2 km grid), 43,076 camera days; the paper pools data across years and between the north (EINP-N) and south (EINP-S) sections, 'because habitats are similar in both areas'. Elk detections 5,790 (summer, April-August, 19,764 camera days), 2,690 (fall, 8,568) and 2,407 (winter, 14,744); elk on all cameras in summer and winter, 41 of 43 in fall. Cameras near hiking trails were moved at least 100 m from the trail; EINP-N has more roads and trails. Bison share the park (plains bison in EINP-N, wood bison in EINP-S) and the paper reports bison-elk daily overlap per season (D4, lowest in summer, highest in winter); it does not test an effect of bison or of human use on elk timing. The Discussion repeats 'Elk activity patterns were crepuscular in all three seasons'; no season is reported as differing for elk. The paper names the species Cervus elaphus; the MDD accepts the North American elk as Cervus canadensis. Bison in the same paper are not filed (plains and wood bison pooled).

source.title: Bison and elk spatiotemporal interactions in Elk Island National Park

quote: Elk activity patterns were clearly crepuscular across seasons.
note: Licence sentence read on the Frontiers PDF: 'This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY).' (the HTML full-text page prints no licence sentence). Byline as printed: Jennifer M. Foca and Mark S. Boyce; citation line begins 'Foca JM and Boyce MS (2022) Bison and elk spatiotemporal interactions in Elk Island National Park.' (Frontiers in Conservation Science volume 3, article 937203). Category is the paper's own wording. Materials and methods print no scientific name for elk; the Abstract, Introduction and Figure 3 caption use Cervus elaphus. MDD species page 1006312 opened: Cervus canadensis Erxleben, 1777, Cervidae, Artiodactyla, 'split from C. elaphus', range includes western Canada. Animals live in a fenced, managed park: free-ranging inside the fence, not captive; two park sections pooled in the analysis as one park population (audit-1366).
